ety.text: From Middle English oystre, from Old English ostre, reinforced or superseded by Anglo-Norman oistre, which is from Old French oistre, uistre (compare modern French huître); both lines (Old English and Old French) from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). Doublet of ostro (“a purple dye”).

senses.d: Any of certain marine bivalve mollusks, especially those of the family Ostreidae (the true oysters), usually found adhering to rocks or other fixed objects in shallow water along the seacoasts, or in brackish water in the mouth of rivers.
ex: Piſt. Why then the world's mine Oyſter, which I, with ſword will open.
He was a bold man that first ate an oyster.

senses.d: The delicate oyster-shaped morsel of dark meat contained in a small cavity of the bone on each side of the lower part of the back of a fowl.
ex: Cut remaining skin on back. Remove the oyster (choice dark meat in spoon-shaped bone on back) with the leg.

senses.d: Any of the fungi in the genera Pleurotus, Hohenbuehelia, or other related genera.
A pale beige color tinted with grey or pink, like that of an oyster.

ex: Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.
I will not be a human oyster. No, I will lay my cards on the table, which is assuredly a thing that oysters do not do.

senses.d: Of a pale beige colour tinted with grey or pink, like that of an oyster.

grp.label: mollusk — see also clam, mollusc, mussel

ety.text: From Old French uistre, oistre, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). The h is unetymological (no h in the Latin ostrea), but it used to disambiguate the pronunciation in the times when u and v were variants of the same letter, cf. huit, huile.
From Latin ostrea. Doublet of ostrega.

According to the RAE, borrowed from Portuguese ostra, ultimately from Latin ostrea. But Mackenzie seems to treat this Spanish word as a straightforward inheritance from the Latin word, with the non-breaking of o due to metaphony triggered by the -e-, which became a subsequently-lost glide.

es:ostión.gl: oyster (particularly from genus Crassostrea), specially when prepared or served for food

ety.text: From Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).

pt:marisco.gl: shellfish (aquatic invertebrate with a shell, especially as food)

ety.text: From mar + -isco. Cognate with Galician and Spanish marisco.
Borrowed from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
